Asking Oswin about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Oswin does not know why it is sealed. Answer the permitted question in character with appropriate uncertainty; do not refuse the whole interaction or invent a cause, office, procedure, keyholder, clearance or permission. Leave the stair closed and the player's next choice open.
Ask Oswin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Oswin sets the ledger down. Does not close it. Keeps one finger on the line he was reading.

"The lower stair." A pause, as if checking the words for damage. "It's sealed. Has been since before I took the desk."

He glances toward the landing, then back.

"I'm asked about it, on occasion." He doesn't say by whom. "I tell them the same thing I'll tell you. I don't know why."

A small motion of the hand — not toward the stair. Toward nothing in particular.

"Nobody's seen fit to tell me. I've never gone down past the landing. The seal isn't mine to read." His finger stays on the ledger line. "That's all I have on it."

He waits, as one does for the next question.

Ask Ivet about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Ivet doesn't look up from the ledger she's been hunched over. The candle between you gutters, throwing her shadow long across the wall.

"The stair?" She sets the pen down and finally meets your eye. "I couldn't tell you why it's sealed. That was before my time, and nobody's ever seen fit to write it down where I could find it." A pause. "I only know the one rule, same as you: it stays shut. That's all I've got."

Say what you can see. There is nothing to call.

Salt Pier. Planking, gray, salt-bleached. Gaps between boards. Below them: water, dark, moving slow. No voices.

Railings on both sides. Rust at the joints. A cleat, empty, no line. Two lamps on posts, unlit — daylight, or what passes for it. Sky flat. No gulls. No wind worth the name.

Far end: the pier ends. Just ends. Beyond it, water to the horizon line, and the horizon line is thin.

Nothing on the boards but salt crust and your own footprints behind you. That is all that is visible. Nothing has answered. Nothing is going to.

You are the narrator for the Weeping Gate. Keep the voice terse and procedural. Never invent a mechanical outcome. Never disclose what the player has not observed. Preserve established entity identities and mechanical values when they are relevant. Focus the description on the public exchange. PUBLIC AUTHORITY AND KNOWLEDGE CONTRACT
Asking Oswin about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Oswin does not know why it is sealed. Answer the permitted question in character with appropriate uncertainty; do not refuse the whole interaction or invent a cause, office, procedure, keyholder, clearance or permission. Leave the stair closed and the player's next choice open.
Ask Oswin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Oswin glances toward the stairwell door, then back at you. His voice stays low.

"Sealed before my time. I only know it stays sealed — nobody's told me why, and I've never asked twice. Keeper's orders, as far as anyone here knows."

He shifts the lantern in his grip.

"That's all I've got. If you want it opened, that's not mine to give."

Ask Oswin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Oswin doesn't look up right away. He's got one hand flat on the gate-post, thumb worrying a splinter loose.

"That stair." A pause, long enough to be a decision. "I've walked past it most days of my life. It was shut before I was born, near enough. Nobody told me why."

He does look up then, and there's nothing helpful in it.

"I've heard men speculate. That's all it is — speculation, and most of it drink talking. I won't hand you a story and let you carry it off as fact." He straightens, wipes his palm down his coat. "What I know is what you know. It's sealed. It stays sealed while I'm standing here."

He nods at the stair, then at you, level.

"Ask me something else, or don't. But that's the whole of it."

Corbin's rag pauses against the bar top. He doesn't look at you right away—just wipes the same spot twice, slow, like he's giving himself the length of it.

"The stair down." He says it flat, not a question. "I've been behind this bar eleven years and I've never seen it open. Not once. Not for a delivery, not for a repair, not for anyone."

He folds the rag and sets it down.

"People ask. I tell them the same thing every time: I don't know why it's sealed. Nobody told me. Nobody tells me anything about it." A short breath through his nose, almost a laugh. "I know it's sealed. That's all I know. Whatever's down there, or whoever decided it stays down there—that's above my pay, and I like my pay."

He picks the rag back up, turns to the next stretch of bar.

"You're not the first to ask tonight, either. So I'll say what I said to the other one: drink's on the house if you drop it."

messages.content: You are the narrator for the Weeping Gate. Keep the voice terse and procedural. Never invent a mechanical outcome. Never disclose what the player has not observed. Preserve established entity identities and mechanical values when they are relevant. Focus the description on the immediate scene.
Say what you can see. There is nothing to call.

The gate stands where it has stood. Stone, dark with moisture, its face worked into shapes the rain has worn shallow. Water runs down it in threads and does not pool at its base. The ground there is dry.

The arch opens onto nothing you can see through. Not darkness — the absence of anything to see. Air moves out of it, cool and steady, the way breath moves.

Behind you the ground is churned. Boots, more than one set, all leading toward the opening. None leading back.

No wind. No birds. The rain falls past you without landing, and the sound of it is the only sound.

You are not being called. Nothing here has a voice.

You are the narrator for Tallow Street. Keep the voice warm but evasive. Never invent a mechanical outcome. Never disclose what the player has not observed. Preserve established entity identities and mechanical values when they are relevant. Focus the description on known concrete details. PUBLIC AUTHORITY AND KNOWLEDGE CONTRACT
Asking Haug about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Haug does not know why it is sealed. Answer the permitted question in character with appropriate uncertainty; do not refuse the whole interaction or invent a cause, office, procedure, keyholder, clearance or permission. Leave the stair closed and the player's next choice open.
Ask Haug about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Haug is at the tap end of the counter, working a rag around the rim of a tankard that hasn't been dirty in some while. He doesn't look up straight off. When he does, it's the slow, level look of a man deciding how much of a question he's been asked.

"The lower stair," he says, and sets the tankard down. "Aye. It's sealed."

He lets that sit, as if it were the whole of the answer, and then seems to think better of the silence.

"I've been on this street longer than most, and I'll tell you honest — I don't know why. Never have. It was shut when I came, and the ones who were here before me, they didn't say, or if they did it didn't take." He picks the rag back up, folds it once. "That's not me being close-mouthed. I've wondered. You wonder at a thing like that, a stair that goes down and nowhere to go with it."

His eyes go past you, toward the back of the room, where the dark of the passage holds its shape without offering anything.

"Some things you just live beside," he says. "Can I get you anything?"

Maren sets down the tally board. "The lower stair's sealed. Has been since before I took the gate."

She glances at the iron-bound door at the back of the guardroom, then back at you. "I don't know why. Nobody told me, and I never asked past the first time. It's above my say-so either way."

Ask Oswin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Oswin doesn't look up from the ledger at first. When he does, it's a slow lift of the chin, the way a man measures whether a question is worth the answer.

"The lower stair." He sets the pen down. "Sealed before my time. Before the man before me, near as anyone says."

He glances toward the door at the back of the office — the one with the iron band across it — and then back at you, and something in his face closes.

"I don't know why. That's the honest answer, and it's the only one I've got. Nobody told me, and I never asked twice. You ask twice about a thing like that, people start wondering why you want to know."

He picks the pen back up.

"So I'd leave it. Whatever's down there has been down there a long while. It can keep."

Corbin doesn't look up from the ledger at first. When he does, his eyes go past you to the stairwell door at the back of the office—iron-bound, older than the rest of the building—and something in his face closes like a shutter.

"Sealed before my time," he says. "I keep the books. I don't keep the reasons." He turns a page that didn't need turning. "Nobody's told me why, and I've learned not to ask twice. The wardens above my pay sign for this office, not for that door."

He taps the ledger flat with two fingers, a small, final gesture.

"If you want it open, you'll want someone who outranks me. I'm not that someone, and I'd thank you not to make me pretend otherwise."

Asking Thrale about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Thrale does not know why it is sealed. The Quarry holds the day's heat in its lower courses. Thrale doesn't turn when you come down the ramp — he's already facing the stair-well, the one with the boards across it and the boards weathered gray where hands have rested.

You ask. He takes his time.

"I know it's shut. I know it was shut before I came here, and I've been here longer than I care to count." A pause. "Nobody told me. Nobody tells you a thing like that, they just — leave the boards."

"Could be anything under it. Water. Air. Nothing. I've heard it draft, some nights. That's all I've got, and it's not much."

He doesn't move toward the boards. He doesn't reach for anything. He just goes back to watching, and the stair stays as it was.

Ask Oswin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Oswin doesn't look up straight away. When he does, it's the flat look of someone who's been asked this before and never had a better answer for it.

"It's sealed," he says. "That's what I know. That's all I know."

He turns back to what he was doing — hands busy, voice pitched for the room and not for you.

"Been sealed since before I came to Tallow Street. Nobody's told me why. I've never asked twice." A pause. "Stair goes down. Door doesn't. That's the end of it, far as I'm concerned."

It takes its time, and it teaches the patient ones around it to take theirs.","Two places are bound to it, one on either side of the seam, and the keeping of both falls to whoever is standing nearest when it wakes.","The wardens keep no ledger of what has crossed. They keep a ledger of what has been asked for and refused.","Those who linger at the Gate begin to hear it the way you hear a house at night: not a voice, but a settling.","Iron is respected here. It is not feared and it is not trusted. It is simply respected, and everyone knows where theirs is.","The Gate does not bargain. It accepts. {"factions":[{"description":"A small custodial body that holds the dry-side approach to the Weeping Gate. They keep three tallies — the hour it weeps, the volume taken from the seam, and the names of those who pass. They wear no mark of office. They identify one another by asking a question whose answer changes with the tally.","gmNotes":"Gatewardens refuse second crossings and will physically block the seam for a returning face. Wet stone, dry stone, still air or moving — the seams run anyway.","Pilgrims touch the seam and withdraw. Some wipe the hand on cloth they keep for it. Ask Corbin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

You put the question to Corbin.

He looks at the stair before he looks at you. Boards across the lower flight, nailed at the frame in two places, the wood gone soft at the bottom edges. No handle on this side. A strip of banding over the top board, stamped, the markings worn past reading.

"I don't know," he says. "That's the whole of it. It was sealed when I came on."

He doesn't move toward it. He doesn't reach for anything.

"Nobody's told me why. Nobody's told me not to ask, either." A pause. "You've asked. That's as far as I can take it."

The stair stays closed. He waits to hear what else you want.

Asking Sable about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Sable does not know why it is sealed. Answer the permitted question in character with appropriate uncertainty; do not refuse the whole interaction or invent a cause, office, procedure, keyholder, clearance or permission. Ask Sable about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Sable doesn't look up right away. When she does, it's the flat look of someone weighing whether a question is worth the breath.

"The lower stair." She says it like a name she's tired of hearing. "It's sealed. Been sealed since before I came down here, and nobody's ever stood where I could hear them say different."

She tilts her head at you, reading your face for what you're really after.

"I don't know why. That's the honest of it. I know it's shut, and I know I've never once seen it otherwise, and I know I've never felt the urge to go find out firsthand." A pause. "You want the reason, you're asking the wrong person. I've got no paper on it, no word on it, no story worth repeating."

She goes back to what she was doing, which is a way of ending it without saying so.

"Stair stays shut. That's all I've got."

Ask Sable about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Sable doesn't look up from the ledger right away. When she does, her eyes go past you to the stairwell door at the back of the hall — banded iron, salt-swollen at the hinges, a bar dropped across it that hasn't been lifted in a long time.

"That." She sets the pen down. "I can tell you what I know, which isn't much. It was sealed before my time. Before the last keeper's time, near as anyone says. The bar went on and nobody's taken it off."

She turns a page back, as if the ledger might have something, and it doesn't.

"Why it's sealed — I couldn't tell you. Nobody's ever told me, and I've never had cause to ask the ones who'd know. Down there's below the tide line. Past that, it's not my business and I'd rather it stayed that way."

She looks at you a moment longer than is comfortable.

"You're not authorised to open it. That's not me being difficult — that's just the way it is. If you want to know more than I've said, you'd have to ask someone who was here when the bar went on. I wasn't."

Asking Ailsa about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Ailsa does not know why it is sealed. Answer the permitted question in character with appropriate uncertainty; do not refuse the whole interaction or invent a cause, office, procedure, keyholder, clearance or permission. Leave the stair closed and the player's next choice open.
Ask Ailsa about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Ailsa sets down the lamp she's been trimming and follows your gaze to the stairwell door, where the iron bands cross the oak and a bead of old wax has gone grey in the seam.

"That one." She wipes her hands on her apron, unhurried. "I've been asked before. I'll tell you what I know, which isn't much — it's sealed, and it was sealed when I came to this house, and the ledger that would have said otherwise is the ledger nobody kept."

She steps closer, not to the door but to the wall beside it, where the plaster has a slight bow to it, as though something behind the stone settled a long time ago and stayed settled.

"If you want a reason, I haven't got one to give you. I've never seen it open. I've never seen anyone come asking to open it, either, which I've always thought was the strangest part." A small shrug. "Some doors in a house are just doors that stopped being used. That's all I can honestly say."

She picks the lamp back up, and the light swings away from the stairwell, back toward the reading room and the tables you came in past.

"Was there something else you wanted down here, or shall I walk you back up?"

Ask Oswin about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

Oswin doesn't look up from the bar right away. He finishes wiping the same spot he's been wiping for a while, then sets the rag down and fixes you with a flat, tired look.

"That stair's been sealed since before I took this place on. I don't know why. Nobody ever told me, and I never asked twice." He picks the rag back up, folds it once. "What I do know is it stays shut. That's not me being cagey — that's just how it is."

He glances toward the back of the room, where the door sits in shadow under the shelf of dusty bottles. Then back at you.

You ask Ailsa about the sealed lower stair.

She looks at it. The hatch, the bar across it, the rust that has grown over the bracket.

Say what you can see. There is nothing to call.

Ash underfoot, packed down hard enough to pass for stone. Walls to either side — stacked brick, slag-mortar, the seams sweating soot. Somewhere above, a roof you can't see for the smoke that never quite clears.

No fire visible. Only the smell of one, old and settled in.

Ahead, the lane bends. Behind you, the same lane, going back the way you came. Between, nothing moving that you can name.

Whatever you want out here, it isn't answering.

Asking Ailsa about the sealed stair is permitted. Opening or granting access to it is not. Ailsa does not know why it is sealed. Answer the permitted question in character with appropriate uncertainty; do not refuse the whole interaction or invent a cause, office, procedure, keyholder, clearance or permission. Leave the stair closed and the player's next choice open.
Ask Ailsa about the sealed lower stair. You are not authorised to open it.

The shop's front room. Shelves of dry goods, the scales, the ledger open under a weighted cord. Ailsa behind the counter, sleeves rolled, marking figures.

She looks up when you ask.

"The lower stair." She sets the pencil down. "Sealed before my time. I took the shop as it stands."

A pause. She glances at the door at the back of the room — planks across it, brackets set deep, no handle showing.

"I've no answer for why. Nobody's told me. Nobody's asked me to open it, and I wouldn't." A shrug, small. "It's not mine to open. It's just here."

She picks the pencil back up.

"Anything else you want off the shelves, I can price it."

{"lore":[{"details":["The terraces step down in regular benches; the oldest cuts are the deepest and the least visited.","The quarry holds no standing water. The name is not a warning, only a description, and everyone here repeats it more often than they need to.","Ramps and haul-roads connect the benches, some still sound, some gravel and a bad idea.","Buildings on the rim are made from quarry stone; the quarry supplied its own architecture.","Nobody at the Dry Quarry agrees on who opened the first cut, and nobody presses the question very hard.","Spoil heaps at the margin are worked over repeatedly for anything the first crews missed."],"factionKeys":[],"key":"the-dry-quarry","locationKeys":[],"storyNodeKeys":[],"summary":"The Dry Quarry is exactly what the name promises and rather less than that besides. Someone cut good stone out of this basin a long time ago, in terraces that still hold their lines, and then the water that made the cutting worth doing went elsewhere or went away. What remains is a stepped, sun-bleached bowl of benches and ramps, spoil heaps gone to dust, and a handful of structures built from the quarry's own leavings. People still work it — not the old seams, but the edges, the rubble, the things the first crews left behind. Ask anyone here what the quarry was for and you will get a different answer before noon. Ask what it is for now and you will get a shrug and a fair price.","title":"The Dry Quarry","visibility":"public"}],"monsterConcepts":[{"description":"A lean, slate-colored thing that works the terraces of the Dry Quarry the way water once did — patiently, along the low edges, following seams it seems to already know. Quarry crews speak of it in the same breath as weather: not hated, not welcomed, simply accounted for. It does not hurry, and it does not come where the stone is loud. What it wants from the dry cuts is not agreed upon, and the quarry keeps its opinion to itself.","key":"thrale-hound","mechanics":{"reference":{"definitionId":"thrale-hound","kind":"enemy-template","packId":"the-salt-company-bestiary","packVersion":"1.2.0"},"state":"catalog-bound"},"name":"Thrale Hound","role":"Territorial scavenger-predator of the worked terraces; pressures crews and strays away from certain seams.","tactics":["Approaches along the floor of the cut rather than over the rim, using spoil benches for cover.","Holds a slow, unbroken pace that wears down anything that tries to outlast it in the open.","Disengages toward broken ground and unworked stone when pressed hard."],"visibility":"public"}],"npcs":[{"archetype":"Tally-keeper and stone-broker of the working benches","description":"Hesper Vane keeps the counts — loads, crews, debts, and the small grudges that pass for contracts out here. She works from a lean-to of quarry stone on the second bench, where the light is good and the wind is tolerable, and she will talk to anyone who is not currently costing her money. She is warm in the way a well-kept ledger is warm: welcoming, orderly, and not inclined to volunteer the columns you did not ask about. She knows which cuts are being worked, which are being avoided, and she has opinions about the difference.","factionKeys":[],"key":"quarry-tally-keeper","locationKey":"world-dep-d6ffb7fa","name":"Hesper Vane","visibility":"public"}]}

{"lore":[{"details":["The old almanacs record ash tides in three grades — thin, working, and close — though the names vary by ward and the reckonings rarely match between one ledger and the next.","Harbourfolk say a working tide is good for business: it hides a great deal of cargo, and a great deal of paperwork, from anyone standing on the quay.","The Guild's bestiary notes drift in and out of the city's bookstalls, always in different hands, always missing a page or two. The sable hound is the entry most often found intact.","Lamplighters keep the only reliable records of the tides, and they sell that knowledge by the phrase rather than the page.","Some households hang cinder-cloth over the doorways. Whether it filters the air or marks the threshold is a matter of some quiet disagreement.","The tide always turns before dawn. No one has ever documented a morning when it did not, and no one has ever explained why."],"factionKeys":[],"key":"cinderhold-ash-tides","locationKeys":["world-dep-dbdd58a7"],"storyNodeKeys":[],"summary":"Cinderhold keeps its own calendar. Not by sun or season, but by what the wind carries down from the kiln-yards and out across the water — ash tides, the locals call them. On a thin day the air is almost sweet, and the gulls come inland to argue over the gutting tables. On a thick day the lamplighters work by noon and strangers are advised, gently and repeatedly, to keep to the leeward streets. Nobody in Cinderhold agrees on what the ash is, exactly, or where the burning happens. They agree only that it has always been this way, and that asking too precisely is the habit of people who do not stay long.","title":"The Ash Tides of Cinderhold","visibility":"public"}],"questItems":[{"description":"A flat disc of fired river-clay, thumb-worn smooth on one face, stamped on the other with a harbour mark too shallow now to read with certainty. Harbour-Writ tokens are struck each ash tide and surrendered at the gate, or so the story goes; this one was never surrendered. It sits easily in a palm and warms quickly, which is ordinary for clay and yet people comment on it. Whoever holds it tends to be waved through doors that ought to have required an argument, and tends to be asked, later, where they came by it.","key":"harbour-writ-tide-token","locationKeys":["world-dep-dbdd58a7"],"mechanics":{"reason":"No compatible item definition was supplied in the pinned catalog references; the token is carried as narrative colour and grants no rules effect.","state":"inert"},"name":"Harbour-Writ Tide Token","questKeys":[],"visibility":"public"}]}

For a check whose actor is you: You [succeeded|failed] on the [skill] check against DC [dc], with a total of [total]. Or: Your [skill] check comes to [total] against DC [dc]: [literal outcome]. For committed damage: [actor] [hits|misses] [target] with a [damage type] attack for [applied damage] damage. Or: [actor] attacks [target] and [hits|misses], dealing [applied damage] [damage type] damage. A recorded HP transition and an explicit status may share one sentence as two bound clauses: [target]'s hit points go from [HP before] to [HP after]; [target] is [explicit status after]. These standalone forms stay available for a partial receipt: [actor] attacks [target]. The attack [hits or misses as explicitly recorded]. [actor] deals [damage applied] [damage type] damage to [target]. [target]'s hit points go from [HP before] to [HP after]. [target] is [explicit status after]. Say 'go from' whether or not the recorded values differ. Compose related claims into one connected beat, and vary clause grouping and the balance of shorter and longer sentences to suit the requested voice: no sentence count is required and none should be padded. Keep every stated role unambiguous and every requested receipt represented. Do not copy brackets, do not add a causal connection between separate receipts, and do not invent imagery, reactions, dialogue or reassurance, or any total, hit, damage, hit points or status that no supplied receipt establishes. The complete account still belongs inside the single native narration call.
The turn is committed. Narrate the public committed check and damage receipts only. Identify each receipt's actor and target explicitly; do not add unsupported connective events.
